Build your movement around the sun
Skip to main contentYour Heatwave Travel Cheat Sheet: What to Pack, Plan & Avoid
While summers once meant carefree days spent frolicking outdoors, today it's record-breaking temperatures that dictate how we experience our destinations. Summer city breaks now demand far more planning, and itineraries require greater caution. Even a leisurely late afternoon by the beach can quickly become exhausting when temperatures soar well above 40°C. Yet, cancelling a summer holiday isn't exactly realistic - nor should it be. Instead, seasoned travellers know there's a smarter way to navigate the heat.
From breathable fabrics, electrolyte sachets and cooling skincare to portable fans, along with a few simple itinerary swaps, the choices you make before and during your trip can make all the difference. Here's how to outsmart soaring temperatures without putting your holiday on hold.
Many cultures have long adapted their routines to avoid the harshest afternoon temperatures. Early mornings - from sunrise until around 10:30 am - offer the most comfortable conditions for walking tours, archaeological sites, and outdoor markets. The period between roughly noon and 4 pm is when temperatures usually peak. Rather than forcing yourself through another museum queue or palace courtyard, schedule activities that naturally provide relief.
“Heat exhaustion often develops gradually. Your cardiovascular system is already under additional strain, yet many travellers wait until they're thirsty to hydrate, spend hours sightseeing in direct sun, or push through fatigue. Listening to your body is a smarter, more sustainable way to stay active while protecting your health,” says Ivana Bruic, fitness expert and founder of Storm Cycling, a cycling studio in Dubai.
For those who like to explore a destination on foot, whether through a morning jog or a sightseeing run, timing becomes everything during a heatwave. “Slow your pace and expect your heart rate to be higher than it would be in cooler conditions. Heat places additional stress on the body, so even experienced runners need to adjust their expectations. One of the biggest mistakes people make is trying to prove they're just as fit on holiday as they are at home,” she says.
Whether it's a hotel gym session or a morning run, many travellers like to stay active on holiday. During a heatwave, however, it's best to dial back your routine rather than push your limits. “I'd absolutely recommend modifying your routine. Heat, travel, disrupted sleep and even mild dehydration place extra stress on the body, so focus on consistency rather than personal bests. Reduce the intensity, shorten your workouts if needed; allow more time for recovery, and swap outdoor runs for indoor strength or lower-impact sessions,” she adds. Packing a set of light, medium and heavy resistance bands makes it easier to stay active without relying on heavy gym equipment.
Food choices can dramatically influence how the body handles heat and take a toll on gut health. “High temperatures, dehydration, disrupted sleep, jet lag and unfamiliar foods can slow digestion and upset the gut microbiome, increasing the likelihood of bloating, constipation, diarrhoea and digestive discomfort,” explains Kate Steckel, a Dubai-based nutrition coach.
